title: The race and the discipline (Hebrews 12:1–13)
hookLine: a cloud of witnesses cheers; lift your drooping hands
carry: lift the hands that hang down
tomorrow: who might be an angel at your door, and how would you know?

cards: Mile three: lungs burning, a cramp coming, and a voice that says just walk. Or a rehab gym, someone gripping the parallel bars, saying I'm done on step seven. So what do you say to someone whose knees have given up?
Hebrews twelve answers with a stadium. The stands are full: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." The crowd is yesterday's list, the named and the nameless.
And down on the track is one runner, carrying far too much.

teach.b: First the crowd calls out: "let us lay aside every weight," and "let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith."

Then today's question: what is the hard part for? Hebrews answers with an old proverb: "whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth." Chastening, in the King James, means training, the hard part of being raised.

And Hebrews doesn't pretend it's pleasant: "Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness." Afterward is the hinge.
Then the coach's shout to a tired team: "Wherefore lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees." That proverb has neighbors.

It lives in Jewish scripture, in the book of Proverbs, as a father's words to his son: don't push away the Lord's correction, for the Lord corrects the one he loves, as a father the child he delights in.
The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, reads that same proverb and speaks of sufferings of love. What's shared: a hard season can come from love and lead somewhere.
The honest difference: Hebrews runs this race looking unto Jesus, who it says endured the cross.

teach.h: LIFT THE HANDS THAT HANG DOWN.
teach.b: Jewish readers hear the proverb with no such runner in view, as wisdom for a life of Torah. One verse, two families reading it.

how: Christians read Hebrews 12 in worship and at hard moments, and the 'cloud of witnesses' is a picture some churches use for the faithful who have gone before.

games.q: what does “the race and the discipline” mean?
o: a patient race, and hard training that bears fruit
a punishment God hands out for doing wrong
a sprint where only the fastest runner wins

games.q: the stadium in Hebrews 12 — tap the pairs.
p: where the father's words come from

s: chastening in Hebrews 12 means punishment for being bad
it's training, the hard part of being raised by a parent who loves you.
the proverb Hebrews quotes is also in Jewish scripture
it's in Proverbs, a father's words to his son, and the Talmud reads it too.
Hebrews says hard training feels joyful at the time
no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: the fruit comes afterward.

games.q: your cousin is cut from varsity and told to train with JV for a season. she asks if it's a punishment. what does the picture in Hebrews 12 suggest?
o: a sign to quit; the race isn't hers.
punishment: someone up there is angry.
games.why: no chastening seems joyous at the time, but grievous; nevertheless afterward it yields fruit. Hebrews reads hard seasons as training, not rejection.

practice: If you're able, stand and walk slowly across the room and back, feeling each knee bend and hold. If walking isn't possible today, press your feet into the floor and lift your hands from your lap to rest open on your knees.
Either way, one line goes with you: lift up the hands which hang down.

wordCard.voice: The race and the discipline. Hebrews twelve: a crowd of witnesses, a runner looking to Jesus, and training that bears fruit afterward.

orig.note: Greek: training, discipline. the word behind 'chastening' in Hebrews 12.

carryVoice: Your line: lift the hands that hang down. Your own, or the tired ones beside you. Until tomorrow.
